brief.head: Monks and tech bros
brief.text: Ajay Shah sees two strands in decluttering: the old ideal of the monk who owns nothing, and the tech bro protecting his brain for intense work. {030-C02}

brief.head: Pigsty superpower
brief.text: Needing a neat room before you can think is a burden, Ajay Shah said. He trains himself to work anywhere, even at a railway station. {030-C16}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on things, minds and mess
lead.head: Less junk, more mess
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah recorded this episode outdoors, and Varma had an explanation ready. “We are decluttering. We have done away with the house. We will not have a roof over our heads anymore. What a great life.” {030-J01}
The joke had a point. For Varma, decluttering is best summed up by the writer Chuck Palahniuk: the things you own end up owning you.
“If we carry too many things,” he said, “everything that we have literally becomes baggage for us.”
Both hosts admitted to mixed feelings. So each set out the philosophy he actually practises.
## The junk in the head
Varma came to the subject through his father’s death. Clearing his late father’s house, full of books, trunks and curios, he decided that his own mind had the same problem.
The clutter that matters most, he argued, is mental: unimportant preoccupations crowding out what matters, and toxic, envious or gossipy people who drain energy. {030-C04}
His remedy is to live in the micro. Where he once wrote ten-item to-do lists and panicked, he now commits to one thing a day. Everything after that is a bonus.

Possessions worry him less. With his reading and writing in the cloud, he enjoys things without being attached. “Every material thing that I have is replaceable,” he said. “What is not replaceable is time.”
Nor does he want life too tidy. Drawing on Tim Harford’s *Messy*, he warned that a life curated into comfort breeds autopilot.
## A bunch of algorithms
Shah described his own approach as “a bunch of algorithms”. Owning things, he said, puts a tax on the mind, so owning less is better.

India, he argued, has an especially big clutter problem. Between about 1991 and 2011, trade barriers fell and incomes rose together, and within twenty years the country went from scarcity to plenty. Its thumb rules about what to buy and keep, he said, are now “a little off”. {030-C10}
His rules for buying: experiment boldly with cheap gadgets, since one good fit pays for many mistakes, and never buy to impress. Then be a “grim reaper” about what goes unused.
Every fabricated object, Shah said, is a statistically improbable arrangement of atoms, and deserves to be used. If he is not using a thing, he gives it to someone who will. {030-C14}
Varma’s caveat: by Sturgeon’s law most of what humans make is crap, and he will not pass on a book he thinks is bad.
## The five and the fifteen
The same thinking applied to people. Most of our emotional energy, Shah said, citing Robin Dunbar, goes to five people and then fifteen more, so we should lavish our attention on them.

With projects, he starts many and finishes few, and calls this the innovation funnel. “For each one line in the resume,” he said, “if you don’t have a hundred lines left behind, then you’re doing something wrong.” {030-C18}
Varma, by his own account an expert procrastinator, saw a danger: the funnel can become an excuse never to execute. He argued for a bias towards action: pick any one idea and do it.

His closing pick, Ken Liu’s *The Paper Menagerie*, was a lesson in decluttered language, and he promised it would make Shah weep. “When we record our next episode, gentle reader,” he said, “Ajay’s eyes will be red.”

second.label: Toxic people
second.head: A part of me dies
second.deck: A friend’s confession in 1990s Bombay taught Amit Varma whom to keep away
body: In the late 1990s, Amit Varma walked out of dinner at Oh! Calcutta in Tardeo, Bombay, with a friend who is now a celebrated and controversial novelist. The friend said: “You know, Amit, every time a friend of mine does well, a part of me dies.” {030-S02}
He was only trying to be clever, but Varma stood in the street, stunned. Many people, he came to see, are like this: they smile and pretend to wish you well, but they don’t.

So he declutters people. He has curated his Twitter feed to keep negativity out, and left WhatsApp groups where people gossip about others all day. {#twitter} “Why shit on others all the time?” he asked.

quote.text: You know, Amit, every time a friend of mine does well, a part of me dies.

second.caption: a friend’s envy

third.head: The marathon that wasn’t
body: Ajay Shah wanted to know how Amit Varma ships an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* and one of *Everything is Everything* every week. Shah put his own share of the second at 30 per cent. {#thirtypercent}
“Badly,” Varma replied. The weekly deadline, he said, is what keeps the shows coming.
His 365 episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen* sound like a marathon, he said, but are really 365 sprints. He does not sleep for two days before a recording, then spends two days recovering. {030-S06}

His resolution for his “second half century” is a real marathon: an hour of writing and two hours of reading every day. Explaining it, he mimed running in his chair. “The rarest object in the world,” said Shah, “a Bengali sprinter.” {030-J11}
third.caption: the 365 sprints

p2.title: The clutter question
p2.deck: Amit Varma tidies his mind, Ajay Shah runs algorithms for his things, and both make room for mess

sections.label: A tidier mind
sections.head: A mind like his father’s house
sections.caption: clearing out his mind
body: Amit Varma admits he is no expert in minimalism. He likes to collect things and owns thousands of books. Clearing his late father’s house in Chandigarh changed how he thought about it. {030-S01}

Nearly everything in that house was junk, he said, probably even to his father. “But we accumulate, accumulate, accumulate.” His own mind, he realised, was the same: crowded with preoccupations that kept him from the one or two things that really matter. {030-C04}
## How we live our days
He has been thinking about the writer Annie Dillard’s line: “How we live our days is how we live our lives.” We fix on grand goals, he said, but life is an accumulation of days. {030-J16}
So his resolution for 2024 is to live in the micro: one thing a day, then chill. On the day of recording, the one thing was shooting three episodes. {030-C03}
Clearing the mind means clearing people too: those with negative energy, always blaming others, entitled. Keep instead, he said, people who make you aspire to be like some facet of themselves.

~ Things are another matter. If his laptop conked off today, he would order another, since his data is in the cloud. Nor would he spurn things to live like a monk; there is, he said, “a certain kind of false virtue” in that. {030-C05}

quote.text: I will do one thing today. And once I have done that one thing, everything is a bonus, but I will chill.

sections.label: The case for mess
sections.head: In praise of a little chaos
sections.caption: the uses of mess
body: Decluttering carries a danger, Amit Varma argued: a life curated so tightly that everything sits in the comfort zone, among familiar voices one already agrees with. {030-C06}
His evidence was the story that opens Tim Harford’s *Messy*. Keith Jarrett, handed a substandard piano in Cologne, improvised a masterpiece because he could not play on autopilot.

Varma craves routine, because he craves discipline. But he also wants “that little bit of unpredictability”. So he has promised the show’s collaborators, Nomsita and Vaishnav, to write by hand in a paper diary every day, because on paper the mind works differently. {#diary}
## Many projects at once

Harford also cites the researchers Howard Gruber and Sara Davis, who found that creative people often work on several projects at once, Darwin among them. Such people, in a phrase Varma learnt from Ajay Shah, are “above the API”. {030-J20}
Shah’s nephew Hemen, in a tiny New York flat, buys almost nothing, because space forces him to be intentional. Varma’s phrase for it, from the poet Ranjit Hoskote, was dancing in chains.

~ Varma himself does not mind books piled on the floor. “I’m not gonna go all Marie Kondo,” he said. If things bring happiness and don’t get in the way, he sees no problem; the clutter that worries him is mental. {030-J21}

quote.text: In a sense we are all dancing in chains. We have constraints all around us, and we dance the best we can

sections.label: Rules for buying
sections.head: Many mistakes, one good watch
sections.caption: buying, boldly and selfishly
body: Owning things, Ajay Shah said, means caring for them, repairing them and protecting them from depreciation, and all of it is a tax on the mind. So he would always rather own less. {#taxonmind}

India’s problem is acute. Since about 1991, trade barriers fell and growth came together, bringing “the wonders of Amazon and AliExpress”. Habits built for scarcity, he argued, now misjudge what to buy and what to keep.
## The Casio dividend
No review can tell you whether a gadget fits your life; only trying it can. Shah’s favourite wristwatch, a Casio, cost him about 1,100 rupees, and he went through many watches to find it. {#casio}
The gap between that price and what he would happily pay is consumer surplus, and it “pays for a lot of mistakes”. So buy cheap gadgets boldly, learn from them, and give away the misses. {030-C11}

Never buy to impress, he said: “Be selfish, live for yourself, and that’s a better life.” For clothes, start with cheap, functional basics. Fashion is not all a con, and technical gear such as merino inners and hiking pants earns its place. {030-C12}
~ He also likes things that last. His body size has not changed since college, he said, so he still wears pants that are thirty years old. {#pants}

quote.text: Gentle reader, that gap between what you paid and what you’re willing to pay is called consumer surplus.

sections.label: Rules for giving
sections.head: Miracles in the cupboard
sections.caption: atoms, watches and the eye
body: As children grow, Ajay Shah said, they discover the glory of biology: every leaf, every fungus, every virus. Edward O. Wilson called this biophilia. {030-R13}

Shah then turned to Richard Dawkins’s *The Blind Watchmaker*. {030-R14} A watch found on a beach implies a maker; the eye is just as improbable but has no designer. Shah flipped it around: the watch, too, is a statistically improbable grouping of atoms, and something magical.
## The sunk cost of things
So he gives away what he does not use. {030-C14} What he paid is a sunk cost and irrelevant. The only questions are whether he uses a thing, and whether someone else would. He dislikes landfills.
He buys gadgets at two or five thousand rupees without noticing, experiments with them, reads the manuals, and passes on the ones that do not fit. {#price}
Amit Varma, reminded of Bob Dylan’s *Every Grain of Sand*, shared Shah’s wonder at nature but not at all things human-made. By Sturgeon’s law, he said, 90 or 95 per cent of everything is crap.

~ Following Tyler Cowen, he will not gift a book he dislikes, though publishers send him many. “Why would I give them a bad book that they might read?” he asked, of readers who manage one or two books a year. {030-C15}

quote.text: We are buying miracles. If you take them back in a time machine, each of these things is a miracle.

sections.label: People and projects
sections.head: Kiss a hundred frogs
sections.caption: the innovation funnel
body: Decluttering matters most at “higher planes of existence”, Ajay Shah said, because the scarcest thing is our cognitive burden. He has trained himself to work anywhere, so that his thinking needs no preconditions. {030-C16}
People come next. Robin Dunbar found we can sustain about 150 meaningful connections, with 40 per cent of our emotional energy going to five people and 20 per cent to fifteen more. {030-R15}
## The innovation funnel

With projects, Shah no longer feels obliged to finish what he starts. Like a sales funnel, he generates many mad ideas, triages instinctively and carries few to completion. Before you find your prince, he said, you have to kiss a hundred frogs. {030-J09}
He has 150 unfinished papers on his laptop. {#papers} He picks one, blocks hours for it, works with full intensity while ignoring everything else, then comes out to triage again.
Amit Varma admired the focus and recalled Steve Jobs telling Jony Ive to learn to say no to things you love. But the funnel, he warned, can become an excuse for expert procrastinators like himself.
~ “It doesn’t matter which of those hundred ideas you take up,” Varma said, “but frickin’ hell take up something and do it.” {030-C21}

quote.text: But for each one line in the resume, if you don’t have a hundred lines left behind, then you’re doing something wrong.

side.boxTitle: The book that argues for mess
side.boxText: Tim Harford’s *Messy* makes the case that creativity comes from being pushed out of your comfort zone. Amit Varma introduced the economist and writer as “also a fellow two-time winner of the Bastiat Prize”. {030-J18}

contQuote.text: We should just accept that we are with our five fifteen people, and we are going to lavish our lives and our attention on them and that’s all there is and there will be nothing more

p3.title: Tales from the clear-out
p3.deck: A house, a piano, a village and a flat: the stories behind the ideas

stories.start: I got to thinking about it seriously a couple of years back
stories.end: And I decided that, okay, I need to declutter my mind as well
stories.caption: his father’s house
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on clearing his late father’s home in Chandigarh
stories.head: Half a room in a big bungalow
body: Amit Varma’s father died during the second wave of Covid. He had been a retired IAS officer, living in a huge bungalow in Chandigarh, and someone had to clear it.
The house was full: thousands of books, trunks, furniture, all kinds of curios. Despite all those rooms, Varma said, his father had basically been living in half a room. {#halfroom}

Varma had no space in his own house for the books. So he brought three friends and told them to pick whatever they wanted. His own rule was to keep only books he wanted to read that were so rare he could not get them anywhere, not even as a downloadable PDF. The rest went.

There was one exception. For ten years his father had urged him to take his fifty-volume set of the *Great Books of the Western World*, and for ten years Varma had refused: in a Bombay apartment, the real estate would cost more than the books.
After his father died, he kept it. When he moved house recently, he gave away hundreds of books but took the set with him. “I’ll never read it,” he said. It is there for sentiment. {030-R21}
What struck him was that most of what filled the house was junk, probably even to his father for most of his life. Then he looked at his own life.
~ “My own mind is like my father’s house,” he said. “It is full of junk, it is full of accumulated crap and it gets in the way.” {030-S01}
stories.why: Clearing the house became a mirror. Years of accumulated preoccupations, Varma realised, were taking up real estate in his mind that should go to what matters, and a physical clear-out turned into a mental one.
stories.postscript: Varma does most of his reading on Kindle. The fifty volumes, he admits, are an artefact.

stories.start: On january twenty seventh, nineteen seventy five, I think it was
stories.end: But he was taken out of his comfort zone. It was messy
stories.caption: the Cologne concert
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a concert that nearly did not happen
stories.head: A broken piano’s finest hour
body: In Cologne in January 1975, Amit Varma said, a 17-year-old named Vera Brandes, the youngest concert organiser in Europe, had booked the legendary pianist Keith Jarrett. The show was sold out.

The hall could not get the piano Jarrett needed and supplied a mini version, “like a half piano”. Its sound did not reach the balcony and some keys did not work. It was pouring, so no replacement could be brought, and Jarrett sat in his car, ready to leave.
Brandes knocked on his window in tears. He agreed to play, for her. Hitting the keys harder, working within a narrower range on an instrument he had never played, he improvised.
~ The album sold three and a half million copies, the largest-selling solo jazz album ever, Varma said, if he remembered correctly. {#cologne}
stories.why: Harford’s thesis, as Varma told it: thrown out of his comfort zone, Jarrett could not coast on autopilot, and genius followed. {030-S03} A life curated into perfect comfort risks losing exactly that. {030-C06}

stories.start: Amitava Kumar in An episode he recorded with me a long time ago
stories.end: I think that we carry our homes around us
stories.caption: Gangauli and home
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a novel, a question and the meaning of home
stories.head: Facing Mecca, thinking of home
body: On *The Seen and the Unseen*, the writer Amitava Kumar once told Amit Varma about a scene in Rahi Masoom Raza’s novel *Aadha Gaon*, set at the time of Partition.
Activists urge a Muslim villager to go to Pakistan. When he prays, he replies, he turns towards Mecca; when he thinks of home, he thinks of his village, Gangauli.
Varma now asks guests: where is your Gangauli? Max Rodenbeck, who grew up in Cairo, said his is the Cairo of his childhood, which no longer exists. {030-S05}

~ Varma has no answer of his own. Cosmopolitan but not rooted, he locates home in whatever surrounds him: his books, his room, the vibe. Marvin Gaye’s *Wherever I Lay My Hat* comes close. “Except that whenever I’ve had a hat, I’ve lost it,” he said. {030-J06}

quote.text: It is a Cairo of my childhood. It no longer exists.

stories.start: my nephew Hemen has a very small flat in New York
stories.end: like Hime, therefore, is dancing in chains. His chains are the constraint of space
stories.caption: a nephew’s tiny flat
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on his nephew’s very small New York flat
stories.head: Small flat, big discipline
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah both live in tiny houses in Bombay. Shah’s nephew Hemen has a very small flat in New York, and it has driven him to extremes of decluttering.
Hemen thinks very hard before buying anything. By default he does not own things; he buys only what really fits his life and his tiny “budget constraint of space”. {030-S04}
Shah added a jab. When people debate a minimum size for affordable housing for the poor, he said, “I’d like to say go visit New York sometime.”
~ Varma saw Hemen as dancing in chains, the phrase he had from the poet Ranjit Hoskote. We all live within constraints, and Hemen’s chains are space. {030-C08}

quote.text: So the shortage of space has driven him to be more intentional around acquiring things.

quiz.q: What is the hosts’ friend Vishal Nevatia’s rule about shirts?
quiz.a: He owns exactly twelve; if a thirteenth appears, one shirt has to go.

quiz.q: In the Minimalism Game, how many things does each player give away on the third day?
quiz.a: Three each: one on day one, two on day two, and so on.

quiz.q: Ajay Shah’s Casio watch cost about 1,100 rupees. What does he call its hidden gift?
quiz.a: Consumer surplus: the gap between what he paid and would happily pay.

quiz.q: Which law did Amit Varma cite to say that most human-made things are crap?
quiz.a: Sturgeon’s law, which says ninety or ninety-five per cent of everything is crap.

quiz.q: With 150 unfinished papers, what two gears does Ajay Shah shift between?
quiz.a: First triage to choose one thing, then a block of hours at full intensity.

quiz.q: Where is Max Rodenbeck’s Gangauli, according to what he told Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Cairo, but the Cairo of his childhood, which he says no longer exists.
